name: Zane Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a building supplies warehouse that stocks the trade counters for the whole region. Timber, plasterboard, bags of cement, boxes of tiles, all the heavy stuff. I'm on goods-in in the mornings, breaking down lorries with a pallet truck, then picking orders for the afternoon vans. It's six till two, and in summer it's flat out while in winter it goes quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real stuff. You can see the pile of timber go out and know it's going into somebody's kitchen. What wears me out is the cement, twenty-five kilos a bag, and the splinters, and the winter when they cut our overtime. My team leader, Craig, says I still stack pallets like a jigsaw with missing pieces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped. At work the lads would say the same, nobody on our floor ever thought a robot was lifting plasterboard. I might comment on a post or two, nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the problem is the same as before: the flat. Priya, my girlfriend, and I have been saving for a deposit for three years. Every year we save a bit more for a deposit, and every year the flats cost a bit more than we saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, take every summer overtime shift I can get, and keep putting about three hundred a month into the deposit pot. We've got around four months of bills in there now. I'd also ask Craig about the forklift licence, because it's an extra pound or so an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about the job, fed up about the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in winter when the overtime goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We tighten up. Priya's a hairdresser, she rents a chair in a salon, so her money goes up and down too. Last January we didn't put anything in the pot for two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for boring stuff, like comparing mortgages or writing a message to the landlord. Priya showed me. I wouldn't trust it with anything big yet.

say: I'd say the AI was **overhyped** and nobody thought robots would lift plasterboard.
I'd add a **comment or two** online, nothing big.
think: My real problem is the **flat deposit**, not AI.
Flat prices **rise faster** than Priya and I can save, year after year.
do: Take every **summer overtime** shift and save three hundred a month.
Ask Craig about a **forklift licence** for the extra pay.
feel: **Fine** about the job but **fed up** about the flat.
S0.quote: Every year we save a bit more for a deposit, and every year the flats cost a bit more than we saved.
fieldNote: Even in a plateau, **housing** is his main pressure.
Both incomes are **seasonal**: his winter overtime and Priya's salon chair.
He uses AI for **small admin**, only after his girlfriend showed him.

steps.text: Take every summer overtime shift on goods-in
Put three hundred a month into the deposit pot
Ask Craig to put him forward for a forklift licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll hit the office long before it hits us. I'd tell people the trade counter guys taking orders on the phone should be worried, not the ones lifting cement. I'd say it at work, maybe in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering, booking lorries, answering the builders' calls, that all goes to AI. My bit is lifting awkward heavy things, and that's hard for a machine. A robot that can lift a wet bag of cement off a broken pallet is further away than the people selling robots think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the forklift licence this year, because that's the next step up and it's still hands-on. I'd use the AI on my phone a bit more, maybe to plan the delivery runs if Craig lets me. And I'd keep saving for the flat, no change there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for the office, mostly okay for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerry on the trade counter. She knows every builder by name and what they ordered last month. The AI would know that too, but builders like her, so maybe she survives longer than people expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change the flat plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. If my job still looks solid, we'd still buy, maybe a year later than hoped. I'd want to see how the company handles the office first.

say: I'd say AI hits the **office and trade counter** long before the floor.
I'd mention it in the **group chat** at work.
think: Ordering, booking and calls go to **AI** first.
Lifting **awkward heavy loads** is hard for robots, so my job lasts longer.
do: Get the **forklift licence** this year as the next hands-on step.
Try AI to **plan delivery runs** if Craig agrees.
Keep saving for the **flat** as planned.
feel: **Uneasy** for office colleagues, mostly **okay** for himself.
S1.quote: A robot that can lift a wet bag of cement off a broken pallet is further away than the people selling robots think.
fieldNote: He judges his **heavy, bulky** work as the slowest to automate.
He'd test AI in a **small, proven** way, true to his steady style.
The **flat purchase** stays on, perhaps a year late.

steps.text: Pass the forklift licence this year
Try an AI app to plan the afternoon van runs
Push the flat purchase back about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready, especially not small builders' merchants. I'd say the government needs to help people move into jobs that are still needed, like building houses. I'd say it at work and share a couple of things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the whole office side is AI, and then by 2031 there are robots that can do what I do. Heavy stuff might give me a year or two longer than the parcel warehouses. I'd rather get a forklift licence now and be the last man driving than wait for a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the forklift licence in the first three months, then start looking at a trade, maybe tiling or plastering, at evening classes. I'd hold off on the flat, because a mortgage with this coming feels mad. I'd keep the savings where they are and stop the holiday fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My chest goes tight thinking about the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we wait on the flat, and she'd be gutted, she's already picked the paint colours. But her hairdressing is safer than my job, people want a person cutting their hair. Maybe she carries us for a bit while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a trade like tiling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every house is different, walls aren't straight, floors aren't level. I've watched our trade customers and half their job is working out what's gone wrong. I can't see a robot doing that by 2031, but I could be wrong.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for small builders' merchants and workers.
I'd ask the government to steer people into **building houses**.
think: The office goes by **2028**, and robots match me by **2031**.
Heavy loads might buy me **a year or two** more than parcel warehouses.
do: Get the **forklift licence** within three months.
Start evening classes in **tiling or plastering**.
Put the **flat purchase** on hold and stop the holiday fund.
feel: **Anxious**, with his chest tight at the thought of the flat.
S2.quote: I'd rather get a forklift licence now and be the last man driving than wait for a letter.
fieldNote: The **flat** is the casualty he feels most, more than the job.
He sees **varied trade work** like tiling as safer than warehouse work.
His girlfriend's **hairdressing** income becomes the household anchor.

steps.text: Pass the forklift licence within three months
Enrol in evening tiling classes at the local college
Put the flat purchase on hold
Stop paying into the holiday fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. I'd tell the younger lads to get a trade while they can. I'd say it at work mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office goes by 2031, robots on the floor by about 2034. The flat is the problem. Signing a twenty-five-year mortgage on a job with eight years left in it doesn't add up. Unless I've got a trade by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence first, then a tiling course over two years, part-time. I'd use AI to work out a budget for the course and the flat together. Once I'm qualified and earning a bit on the side, then we'd look at buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. More busy than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earning on the side. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small jobs at weekends, splashbacks and bathroom floors for friends and family first. Priya's clients are always asking if she knows anyone. That's half my customers sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing a course after a six o'clock start. I'm knackered by four. I'd have to give up the Thursday football, and that hurts.

say: I'd say five years is enough **if people start now**.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **get a trade** while they can.
think: Robots reach the floor by about **2034**, eight years away.
A **twenty-five-year mortgage** on that job doesn't add up without a trade.
do: Get the **forklift licence**, then a part-time **tiling course** over two years.
Use AI to **budget** for the course and the flat together.
S3.quote: Signing a twenty-five-year mortgage on a job with eight years left in it doesn't add up.
fieldNote: The **mortgage decision** is where AI timing bites hardest for him.
He'd build a **weekend tiling** side business through his girlfriend's clients.
Giving up **Thursday football** is the sacrifice he names.

steps.text: Take a two-year part-time tiling course
Use AI to budget the course and flat together
Tile splashbacks for friends at weekends
Wait to buy the flat until qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far enough off to plan for properly. People should use the time to learn something solid. I'd say that at work and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to learn tiling properly, and a bathroom floor in an old house is a nightmare for any robot. By 2039 I could have my own little firm. That sounds better than what I'd have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Priya in the next year or two, because the job looks safe for a while. I'd do the forklift licence, then the tiling course a bit later. I'd keep saving and see how the first AI changes go in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, with something to watch in the distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy the flat in this one. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years plus three is longer than most people keep their first flat anyway. By the time robots are lifting cement, we could sell or I'd be tiling. It's a risk I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you speed up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our office got cut quicker than people expect. If Kerry on the trade counter lost her job, I'd take that as my warning.

say: I'd say it's **far enough off** to plan properly.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn something solid** while they have time.
think: Ten years is enough to **learn tiling** properly before robots arrive.
By 2039 I could run **my own small firm**.
do: **Buy the flat** with Priya within a year or two.
Do the **forklift licence**, then tiling later, while saving steadily.
feel: Fairly **settled**, with something to watch in the distance.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to learn tiling properly, and a bathroom floor in an old house is a nightmare for any robot.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **buy the flat**, unlike the faster scenarios.
His warning sign would be the **trade counter** losing staff.
He imagines owning a **small tiling firm** by 2039.

steps.text: Buy the flat with Priya within two years
Pass the forklift licence, then start tiling later
Keep saving three hundred a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It lands right when we'd want to buy, and I'd have no trade yet. What would help is cheap evening courses in trades and some honesty from companies about which jobs are going and when.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about housing. Everyone my age is stuck renting, and this just makes it worse. I'm not against robots. I'm against signing for a flat and then finding out my job had a sell-by date.

headlineQuote: I'm not against robots. I'm against signing for a flat and then finding out my job had a sell-by date.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old goods-in worker** at a building supplies warehouse, still learning to stack pallets well.
He and his girlfriend Priya have saved for a **flat deposit** for three years.
He is **pragmatic** and moves once things are proven, with tiling as his planned trade.
His mood stays **uneasy** in slow scenarios and becomes **anxious** once robots could arrive by 2031 or 2034.
AI timing mostly changes **when he buys** the flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving just as they want to buy and before he has a trade.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **evening trade courses** and honesty from companies about which jobs go when.
